name: Tomas Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tomas Torres, 58. Rosa and I own Ridge Farm, 110 acres: 300 ewes, thirty beef cattle, oats and silage. On the side I do contract work for the neighbours, baling with my own round baler and mapping fields with a drone. Rosa keeps the books for us and a few other farms. Our son Mateo is an electrician who helps me at weekends, and our daughter Clara is a nurse. We've one grandson, Leo, who's nine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sheep in the morning, then it depends: in summer I'm baling for six or seven neighbours till midnight. I use the AI every day, for quotes, for planning the baling route, for reading the drone maps, even for asking why the baler knotter keeps missing. I love a job done well and paid on time. What wears me out is the loan on the baler, £38,000 over five years, and how thin we are: maybe two weeks of money after the payments. Everything we earn goes back into machines. That's how my father did it, and that's how I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? Then I've been using it right, a bit at a time. Fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool for a working man, nothing more. I'd say it at the mart and to the young lads who ask me about the drone. I'd post the odd drone video, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes nothing for my worries. The baler loan, the lamb price, two weeks in the bank. If I break down in July, I lose the contract work and still owe the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep using the AI for quotes and routes, because it saves me two evenings a week. I'd put £150 a month aside for baler repairs, so a breakdown doesn't sink us. And I'd chase every late payer, politely, by text the AI writes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit tight in the chest when I think of the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the worst late payer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't name him. A big farmer, owes me £2,400 since August. He'll pay, they always do, but he knows I can't afford to wait and he takes his time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young farmers about the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use what saves you time and ignore the rest. Nobody gives you anything in farming. A tool that does your evening paperwork is worth more than a grant you have to beg for.

A **breakdown in July** would cost the contract work and still leave the debt.

Save **£150 a month** for baler repairs.
Chase **late payers** politely by AI-written text.
feel: Mostly **steady**, but **tight** in the chest about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning, buying, booking. That's half my contracting work. And robots slower. Good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for the man who moves first, and I'd say move. I'd tell people at the mart the farmers who wait will be paying the ones who didn't. It's a free country, everyone chooses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. AI booking and quotes let one man run twice the contract jobs. The risk is the big contractors, like Greenway, doing the same with ten times my money. I'd have to be quicker and cheaper and more local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI booking page so farmers book baling and drone mapping themselves. I'd buy a second drone, maybe £6,000 second-hand, for spraying spot weeds. And I'd train Mateo to fly it, so we can do two farms at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. Like the first day of harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: £6,000 with two weeks in the bank. How would you pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finance, over three years, and I'd only do it with three farmers signed up first. I don't buy a machine until the work is waiting for it. That's my one rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rosa say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa would say, Tomas, another loan? Then she'd do the sums and say all right, but this is the last one. It's never the last one.

I'd tell the mart that farmers who wait **pay** the ones who didn't.
think: AI booking lets one man run **twice the jobs**.
Big contractors with **ten times my money** could do the same.
do: Set up an **AI booking page** for baling and drone mapping.
Buy a **second drone** for about £6,000 on three-year finance.
Train son Mateo to **fly the drone** so we cover two farms.
S1.quote: I don't buy a machine until the work is waiting for it. That's my one rule.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a **business opportunity** for his contracting.
His competition worry is **big contractors** with deeper pockets.
He has a firm rule: **work first**, then buy the machine.

steps.text: Set up an AI booking page for baling and drone jobs
Buy a £6,000 second-hand spraying drone on finance
Train son Mateo to fly the drone at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, then robots by 2031. I'd be 63, and I'd want one of those robots, not to lose to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get in early or get left behind, and I'd mean it for every farmer I know. I'd say the government should get out of the way and let farmers buy what they need. No handouts, just fewer rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the AI in 2028 does my planning and quotes, fine. The robots in 2031 are the race. Whoever owns a field robot first in this valley gets all the contract work, and that's either me or Greenway. With two weeks in the bank and the baler loan, I can't buy one on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd make Mateo a partner in the business, so we can borrow together against both our names. I'd get on every dealer's list for the first field robots, and plan to lease one in 2031. We'd cut everything at home that isn't the business. And I'd sell the old tractor to clear the baler loan early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, and hungry. It's a gamble, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Greenway gets there first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd become their local man, running their robots on our side of the valley. I'd hate it, being someone's man. But it's better than sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mateo think about being a partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Mateo says yes if he can wire the robots and I deal with the farmers. He's right, he's better with wires and I'm better with stubborn old men.

say: I'd tell every farmer to **get in early** or get left behind.
I'd say the government should allow **fewer rules**, not handouts.
think: Robots in 2031 start a **race** for the valley's contract work.
With two weeks in the bank, I **can't buy** a robot alone.
do: Make Mateo a **business partner** to borrow together.
Join every dealer's **waiting list** to lease a field robot in 2031.
Sell the **old tractor** to clear the baler loan early.
S2.quote: My son Mateo says yes if he can wire the robots and I deal with the farmers.
fieldNote: He treats the robot date as **a race**, not a threat, though money limits him.
He'd bring his son in as **partner** to borrow, a family solution.
His fallback is working for **a big contractor**, which hurts his pride.

steps.text: Make son Mateo a partner so they can borrow together
Join dealer waiting lists to lease a field robot in 2031
Sell the old tractor to clear the baler loan early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That gives me time to get the money right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work. I'd say farmers should train their own sons and daughters, not wait for a government scheme. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I like this one. The baler loan is paid off in 2029, the AI arrives in 2031, and by 2034 Mateo and I could have the money for a robot lease. I'd be 66, still running the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the baler loan on time and save for a deposit. I'd take a course in running field robots once the first dealer runs one, with Mateo. And I'd start a small robot hire service for the neighbours, so the robot pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. A bit restless, wanting to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the hire service charge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet, that's the honest answer. Maybe by the acre, like baling. I'd ask the AI to work it out against what Greenway charges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandson Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandson Leo to learn to fix things, because whoever fixes the robots will never be out of work. He'd rather play football, of course.

I'd say farmers should **train their own children**, not wait for a scheme.
think: The **baler loan** clears in 2029, before AGI in 2031.
By 2034 we could afford a **robot lease** with Mateo.

Start a **robot hire service** for neighbours.
S3.quote: I'd tell my grandson Leo to learn to fix things, because whoever fixes the robots will never be out of work.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **clear debt** first, which eases his mood.

His traditional view shows: **families train their own** rather than wait for government.

steps.text: Clear the baler loan and save a robot lease deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots by 2039. Then this is Mateo's race, and I'm the coach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who wants to work, and there's no excuse for being left behind. I'd say it at the mart. Some would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for us. I'm 71 in 2039, the business would be Mateo's by then, and he'd own a robot fleet instead of renting himself out. My own money stays thin, but the farm's future looks better, not worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming and contracting as now. I'd hand Mateo half the contracting business by 2030 and teach him the customers. And I'd keep putting the AI to work on the quotes and the books, so Rosa can cut her hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Proud, even. It feels like building something for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your own money stays thin. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. But Rosa and I have the farm and the sheep, and Mateo would never see us short. That's family. That's what it's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd fear in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rules. If the government decides only big firms can run field robots, for safety or whatever, men like Mateo are finished. I'd fight that.

I'd say it at the **mart**, knowing some would roll their eyes.
think: By 2039 the business is **Mateo's**, owning a robot fleet.
My **money stays thin**, but the farm's future looks better.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be racing big contractors with two weeks in the bank. What would help is fair access to finance for small firms and no rules that keep robots for the big boys only. And apprenticeships, so young people learn to fix the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'll own the robots. That's the whole question. If the farmer owns the machine, the farmer's free. If the farmer rents the machine from a company, the farmer's a worker again.

headlineQuote: If the farmer owns the machine, the farmer's free. If the farmer rents the machine from a company, the farmer's a worker again.
portrait: Tomas, 58, owns **Ridge Farm** with his wife Rosa and runs a **contracting** side business.
He reinvests everything into machines, leaving about **two weeks of savings** and a baler loan.
He uses **AI daily** and sees robots as a race he wants to win, with son Mateo.
He favours **fewer rules** and family self-reliance over government help.
He's **anxious** at two years, uneasy at five, and **calm** with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, racing big contractors with only two weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: Fair **finance** for small firms and no rules reserving robots for big ones.
**Apprenticeships** so young people learn to fix machines.
